title: Devaki Asks for Her Slain Sons
story:
In Dwaraka, everyone told the story of the boy who had come back from the dead. But for Devaki it was never a story.

Years before, when Krishna and Balarama had finished their studies, their teacher had asked for his fee: his own son, dead and gone, was to be brought back to him. The two brothers had gone to the world of the dead and done it, returning the boy to his father's arms. People marveled at the tale; it was told at feasts and retold to children. And Devaki heard it the way a woman hears a thing when it touches her own loss.

She had borne eight children, and six of them she had never seen grow. Kamsa, her own brother, had killed them one by one as soon as they were born, for he lived in fear that one of her sons would grow up to take his kingdom and his life. She had held each child only long enough to lose it. She had never watched one of those six take a step or speak a word; her whole memory of them was grief, worn smooth by years of silence. In Dwaraka, surrounded by palaces and grandsons, she had learned not to speak of them. The loss did not diminish with distance; it simply became the shape of her days, a room in the house of her mind she had learned to walk past quickly.

But the story of the teacher's son undid that silence. A father had wept for one dead boy, and his sons had brought him back. She had wept for six, and no one had ever brought them back, not the priests with their rites, not the years with their healing, not even the gods. The tale that made everyone else marvel made Devaki's old wound open again, and this time she did not turn away from it.

She went to Krishna and Balarama with tears on her face, and she did not demand; she asked. "You two are the lords of the masters of yoga," she said. "When your teacher commanded you, you went to the world of the dead and fetched back a son, long dead, and returned him to his father. That was the fee he asked, and you paid it. Grant my wish the same way. Bring back my sons, the ones the Bhoja king slew. I held each of them only long enough to lose him."

The two brothers looked at their mother. They did not tell her it was impossible. They did not say that the dead cannot be returned, that the years cannot be undone. They had fetched a dead son once, for a teacher's fee. She was their mother, and her wish was older than the palace she lived in, older than the kingdom, older than the grief she had carried all these years.

And in their silence Devaki understood that she had been heard. Whatever the two lords of yoga intended, they had not refused her; they had not turned away. Standing before her sons in the bright halls of Dwaraka, with the tears still on her face, she felt the weight of years lift just a little, like a door opening in that room of her mind she had walked past for so long. For the first time in years, she let herself hope.
reflection: What is striking is how quiet the request is. Devaki does not rage or reproach; she reminds her sons of what they once did for a stranger's son and asks, almost gently, for the same for her own. In this telling, grief does not thunder; it remembers, and asks.
next_story_tease: To answer her, the two brothers would descend beneath the world, to the kingdom of the daitya king Bali.
hero_scene: Devaki, tears on her face, stands before Krishna and Balarama in the palace at Dwaraka, her hands clasped as she asks them to bring back the six sons Kamsa slew, and the two brothers look at their mother in silence.
visual_elements: Devaki with tears on her face
mood of grief turned to quiet hope
